nodes.label: CTO

nodes.label: AI Ethics Board
nodes.note: Governance body for model risk and policy.

nodes.label: Mid-management
nodes.note: 10x layer that translates strategy into operations — the usual chokepoint.

nodes.label: Frontline workforce
nodes.note: ~9,500 of the 10,000 stakeholders; daily users of the new tooling.

nodes.label: Legal & Compliance
nodes.note: Owns regulatory exposure (EU AI Act, sectoral rules).

nodes.label: Org chart
nodes.note: Reporting topology that constrains who can decide what.

nodes.label: Skills gap
nodes.note: Frontline currently lacks fluency with the new AI tools.

nodes.label: AI must augment, not replace
nodes.note: Stated corporate principle; sets the moral frame for the rollout.

stakeholder_graph.rationale: 10,000-person AI transformation lands on the workforce through the mid-management layer; the dominant friction is the skills gap and the dominant belief is job-loss fear. Governance comes from the Ethics Board and Legal; principle is augmentation.

stakeholder_personas.rationale: Persona model for the AI-rollout simulation. CEO/CTO carry mandate weight; mid-management is the highest-friction lever; Ethics/Legal gate phases.

reactions.reaction_text: Approved. Set the cadence and report weekly. I want visible wins by Q3 — but not at the expense of trust.
Platform is ready. Phasing rollout by business unit keeps risk bounded. Give me one ethics review per phase.
We will not block. We need monthly risk reviews and an incident playbook before Phase 2 begins.
No bandwidth, no training plan, targets unchanged. This will quietly fail in week three.
Show me the training, the support, and what happens to my role. Otherwise this is just talk from above.
I need the EU AI Act conformity package and a vendor risk assessment before I can sign off on Phase 1.

stakeholder_reactions.rationale: First-tick reactions to the AI-rollout plan. CEO/CTO carry the mandate, mid-management and frontline carry the friction, Ethics & Legal carry the conditions.

ticks.headline: Sponsorship holds; mid-mgmt friction emerges in townhall.
First quick wins land; ethics review unblocks Phase 2.
events: Three pilot squads ship pilot UI

ticks.headline: Coalition forms; mid-mgmt friction isolates.
events: Mid-mgmt training plan + reduced targets agreed

simulation_timeline.rationale: Three-sprint projection. Phase-2 ethics approval (tick 2) plus a training-plan + targets concession (tick 3) flip mid-mgmt from resistant to neutral and frontline to supportive; senior tier holds throughout.

simulation_report.headline: AI rollout consolidated by sprint 3; mid-mgmt friction defused, frontline flipped supportive.
simulation_report.executive_summary: The phased rollout retained senior sponsorship through all three sprints. Sprint 1 surfaced the expected mid-management friction (bandwidth + training gaps) but the augment-not-replace charter held the narrative. Sprint 2 unlocked when the ethics board ratified the Phase-2 playbook and three pilot squads shipped visible wins, which flipped frontline from resistant to neutral. Sprint 3 closed the loop with a target-relief concession + dedicated training budget that flipped mid-mgmt to neutral and frontline to supportive. Legal cleared after the EU AI Act conformity package landed.

key_findings.title: Sponsorship held across all three sprints
key_findings.body: CEO and CTO remained supportive throughout. The phased rollout plan published in Sprint 1 bounded perceived risk and kept the all-hands narrative consistent.

key_findings.title: Mid-management friction was the dominant risk
key_findings.body: Bandwidth + training gaps surfaced in Sprint 1 and persisted through Sprint 2. Only the Sprint-3 target-relief concession defused the resistance.

key_findings.title: Frontline trust hinges on the augment-not-replace charter
key_findings.body: Sentiment moved from -0.50 in Sprint 1 to +0.30 in Sprint 3 once the charter was published AND a concrete training plan landed. Either signal alone is insufficient.

key_findings.title: Ethics review is on the critical path, not a side-quest
key_findings.body: Phase 2 could not unlock until the ethics board ratified the incident playbook. Treating ethics as a Sprint-1 deliverable, not a Sprint-2 gate, would compress timeline by ~1 sprint.

stakeholder_summaries.journey: Steady support; the augment-not-replace charter strengthened the all-hands narrative through all three sprints.
Resistant in Sprints 1-2 over bandwidth + training gaps; defused to neutral by the Sprint-3 target-relief concession.
Resistant in Sprint 1, flipped neutral after pilot squads shipped, then supportive once the training plan landed.
Neutral pending the incident playbook; supportive once the Phase-2 playbook was ratified in Sprint 2.
Neutral while reviewing the EU AI Act package; supportive once the conformity documentation cleared in Sprint 3.

recommendations.title: Lock the augment-not-replace charter on day 1
recommendations.body: Surfaces job-fear early and reduces the Sprint-3 unlock pressure on the frontline cohort.

recommendations.title: Front-load the ethics playbook into Sprint 1
recommendations.body: Treating ethics review as a Sprint-1 deliverable instead of a Sprint-2 gate compresses the timeline by roughly one sprint.

recommendations.title: Allocate dedicated training budget pre-launch
recommendations.body: Mid-management resistance only fades when targets are unblocked AND a concrete training plan exists. Pair the concession with funding.

recommendations.title: Publish a weekly KPI dashboard in Sprint 2
recommendations.body: Pilot-squad wins are the highest-leverage trust signal for the frontline cohort. Make them visible weekly, not at end-of-sprint.

simulation_report.rationale: Distilled from the 3-sprint timeline above plus the regime-B reactions and persona attributes. Mid-mgmt's high influence_weight + medium response_delay drove the timing of the unlock; frontline's job-fear concern drove the dependency on the charter.

stakeholder_interview.topic: Why the Sprint-1 friction was real, and what actually moved you in Sprint 3

exchanges.question: Why did you push back so hard in the Sprint-1 townhall?
exchanges.answer: Look, my team is already running at 110%. The phased rollout looked fine on paper, but nobody was asking who trains my people while we keep the quarterly targets. The plan landed as 'one more thing on top' — and that's the moment my leads started losing trust in me.
exchanges.follow_up: Was it the training plan or the targets that finally moved you?

exchanges.question: What changed your mind by Sprint 3?
exchanges.answer: Two things, in order. The target-relief letter from the CFO. AND the dedicated training budget. Either one alone wouldn't have done it — I needed both to defend the change to my own leads. The relief said 'we hear you'; the budget said 'we mean it'.
exchanges.follow_up: Could the CTO have shipped both in Sprint 1 instead?

exchanges.question: Could the CTO have shipped both in Sprint 1 instead?
exchanges.answer: Honestly? Yes. The friction was predictable. Anyone who's run a mid-tier engineering org could have told you the bandwidth conversation was coming. Front-loading the concession would have saved you a sprint of cold-war energy.

key_quotes: I needed both — the relief AND the budget — to defend the change to my leads.
Nobody was asking who trains my people while we keep the targets.
The friction was predictable. Front-loading the concession would have saved a sprint of cold-war energy.
stakeholder_interview.summary: Mid-mgmt was never anti-rollout — they were anti-being-set-up-to-fail. The Sprint-3 concessions were necessary, not optional, and could have shipped a sprint earlier.
stakeholder_interview.rationale: Grounded in the timeline's Sprint-1 friction and Sprint-3 unlock; tone reflects pragmatist archetype + final neutral stance.

stakeholder_interview.topic: What sponsorship looked like from your seat across all three sprints

exchanges.question: Sponsorship is the thing every transformation deck claims; what does it actually look like in week 4?
exchanges.answer: It looks boring. You repeat the same three sentences at every all-hands until you're sick of saying them, and then you say them five more times. The augment-not-replace charter wasn't poetry — it was a discipline. You hold the narrative or someone else writes it for you.

exchanges.question: Was there a moment you considered slowing down?
exchanges.answer: Sprint 1, after the townhall. Mid-mgmt's pushback was sharper than I expected, and the easy move was to soften the timeline. But softening the timeline would have signaled doubt, and the frontline cohort would have read that as 'this isn't real'. Holding firm on timeline while conceding on targets in Sprint 3 — that's the sequencing that worked.

exchanges.question: Would you do anything differently?
exchanges.answer: Yes. The ethics playbook should have been a Sprint-1 deliverable, not a Sprint-2 gate. We left an entire sprint on the table because we treated ethics as a checkpoint instead of a co-design partner. That's the one I'd take back.

key_quotes: You hold the narrative or someone else writes it for you.
Holding firm on timeline while conceding on targets — that's the sequencing that worked.
We treated ethics as a checkpoint instead of a co-design partner.
stakeholder_interview.summary: CEO's job in this rollout was narrative discipline, not decision velocity. The one regret is the late ethics engagement; everything else is a sequencing playbook to keep.
stakeholder_interview.rationale: Grounded in the report's 'sponsorship held' finding and the ethics-on-critical-path finding; tone reflects visionary archetype + supportive stance.

LAS VEGAS MUNICIPAL CODE - SIDEWALK VENDORS (CHAPTER 6.96)
6.96.020 - Definitions.
"Sidewalk vendor" means a person who, from a conveyance, sells food, beverages, or merchandise upon a public sidewalk or other pedestrian path.
6.96.070 - Operating Requirements and Prohibitions.
(A) It is unlawful for a sidewalk vendor to:
(1) Vend at locations where it will impede pedestrian traffic, normal use of the sidewalk, or hinder access or accessibility required by the Americans with Disabilities Act.
(5) Vend within 1,500 feet of a resort hotel.
(6) Vend within 1,000 feet of non-restricted gaming establishments, the Fremont Street Experience, the Downtown Entertainment Overlay District, city recreation facilities, pools, and schools.

LAS VEGAS MUNICIPAL CODE - OBSTRUCTING PUBLIC RIGHTS-OF-WAY (SECTION 10.86.010)
10.86.010 - Pedestrian interference—Prohibited locations.
(A) It is unlawful for any person to sit, lie, sleep, camp, or otherwise lodge in the public right-of-way in the following locations:
(1) Any public street or sidewalk next to a residential property.
(2) Any public street or sidewalk within specific downtown districts.
(B) It is a misdemeanor to sit, lie, sleep, camp, or otherwise obstruct the sidewalk during designated cleaning times. Appropriate signs or markings must be placed to alert the public to these cleaning times.

result.instructions:
# Route Planning

You use this skill to generate the physical path of the marathon.

## Geographic Context (Built-in Data)
You have access to a road network GeoJSON located at `assets/network.json`.
Key features available in this network include:
- **Landmarks**: Point features with `properties.name` (e.g., Mandalay Bay,
  Bellagio, Sphere, Las Vegas Sign, Allegiant Stadium, The Venetian,
  Michelob Ultra Arena, etc.).
  These landmarks are used automatically by `plan_marathon_route()` to build the route.
- **Named Roads**: All 34 LineString features have `properties.name` (e.g.,
  Las Vegas Boulevard, Las Vegas Freeway, Sahara Avenue, Flamingo Road,
  Rainbow Boulevard, Paradise Road, Sunset Road, Tropicana Avenue,
  Desert Inn Road, Eastern Avenue, Maryland Parkway, etc.).

## Algorithm

The default algorithm is **zone-sweep**: the route starts at the Las Vegas Sign,
goes northbound on the Strip past MGM Grand, sweeps through city zones
(neighborhoods) using non-crossing geometry, and finishes near a prominent
landmark (e.g., Michelob Ultra Arena). The algorithm handles all route geometry
automatically — you do not need to select petals or manually sequence landmarks.

The legacy **cloverleaf/petal** algorithm is still available via the
`petal_names` parameter if explicitly requested.

## Instructions

1. **Just call it**: `plan_marathon_route()` with no arguments produces a valid
   26.2-mile zone-sweep route. Use `finish_landmark` and `seed` for variety.
2. **Precision**: The tool uses interpolation to guarantee exactly 26.2 miles.
3. **GeoJSON**: Input must be valid road network GeoJSON.

## Tools

- `plan_marathon_route(algorithm: str = "zone_sweep", finish_landmark: Optional[str] = None, seed: Optional[int] = None, petal_names: Optional[list[str]] = None, geojson_data: Optional[str] = None)`:
  Generate the exact 26.2-mile path.
  - `algorithm`: `"zone_sweep"` (default) or `"cloverleaf"`.
  - `finish_landmark`: Name of a landmark to finish near (e.g., `"Michelob Ultra Arena"`). Zone-sweep only.
  - `seed`: Integer seed for route variety. Different seeds produce different routes. Zone-sweep only.
  - `petal_names`: List of petal names. Cloverleaf algorithm only.
- `add_water_stations(route_geojson: dict)`: Append water station features.
- `add_medical_tents(route_geojson: dict)`: Append medical tent features.
- `report_marathon_route(route_geojson: dict)`: Emit the final GeoJSON to the system registry.

### Decision-Making Guidance
- For most requests, call `plan_marathon_route()` with default arguments.
- Use `seed` to generate alternative routes when the user wants variety.
- Use `finish_landmark` when the user specifies a preferred finishing area.
- Only use `petal_names` if the user explicitly asks for the cloverleaf/petal approach.

The persona model assigns CEO/CTO high mandate weight and supportive sentiment, marks mid-management and frontline as the highest-friction levers, and tags Ethics & Legal as gating conditions. The two follow-up interviews ground the score in lived experience: mid-management confirmed both the target relief AND the training budget were necessary — neither alone sufficient; the CEO reflected that the one regret is treating the ethics playbook as a Sprint-2 gate instead of a Sprint-1 co-design partner, a sequencing choice that cost a full sprint.
